title: Elasticity probe and trace-driven microbench playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a practical playbook for running focused elasticity probes and trace-driven microbench experiments that target three interacting subsystems: kernel selection, scheduler behavior, and KV cache effectiveness. The goal is to create lightweight, reproducible checks that catch performance regressions earlier than full E2E suites, provide actionable signal about which subsystem regressed, and generate compact artifacts for postmortems.

Scope and constraints:
- Scope: single-node and small multi-node GPU serving variants representative of our Dedicated/Private tiers. Not intended to replace large-scale capacity tests.
- Models: prioritize Llama-like and Opt-style families with 8k and 32k context variants. Include one seq2seq-ish model for attention pattern variance.
- Workloads: warm and cold cache, prefix-heavy (chat-like), and long-generation streams.
- Constraints: keep per-run time under ~30 minutes to enable CI integration.

High-level approach:
1) Use trace-driven microbench harness: replay representative traces with controlled arrival timings rather than fully synthetic infinite loops.
2) Probe elasticity: create short scenarios that increase request concurrency and token churn to exercise scheduler scaling and kernel-switch paths.
3) KV cache stress tests: measure cache hit/miss behaviors and quantify token-level cost and latency impact.
4) Combine kernel profiling (light-weight sampling) with end-to-end latency/throughput metrics to localize regressions.

Harness components (roles):
- driver: orchestrates replay, emits meta events (start/stop/warmup markers) and records timestamps.
- worker: runs the actual runtime under test; instrumented to export micro-metrics (kernel selection counts, batch sizes, queue lengths, KV hits/misses).
- trace repository: small set of canonical traces (chat_short, chat_long_prefix, batch_mix_peak, seq2seq_synth).
- collector: pulls logs, microtraces, perf counters and consolidates into a single artifact tarball.

Trace selection and synthesis rules:
- Prefer small-to-medium traces (2–30 requests, 1–20 tokens per request) for quick iterations.
- Each trace must include: client-side timestamps, user prefix length, target generation length, function-calling markers if applicable.
- Derive synthetic variations by random jittering arrival times (+/- 20%), substituting prefix lengths from distribution observed in production (p10/p50/p90), and toggling KV cache warmness.
- Maintain a catalog file (trace_manifest.csv) with tags: kernel-sensitive, kv-sensitive, scheduling-sensitive.

Microbench experiment matrix (examples):
- Baseline: 1 client, cold KV cache, single-stream, default kernel set.
- Kernel stress: 4 concurrent clients, long sequences, trigger kernel fallback path (quantization+fp16->int8 switching).
- Scheduler churn: ramp clients 1->16 over 60s, observe queue depth and dispatch latency.
- KV effectiveness: send repeated prefixes to measure hit ratio and delta in token latency.
- Mixed: interleave small prompts and huge prompts to force heterogeneous batching behavior.

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- request-level: request_id, start_ts, first_token_ts, last_token_ts, tokens_generated, status
- host-level: GPU util, memory, temperature, kernel_name per invocation, kernel_latency_ms, batch_size
- kv-metrics: kv_lookup_count, kv_hit_count, kv_evictions, average_kv_latency_ms, cache_warm_percent
- scheduler: queue_length_samples, dispatch_latency_ms, avg_batches_per_second, idle_worker_count
- derived: p50/p90/p99 latency (generation and tail), tokens/sec per GPU, kernel-switch rate, end-to-end tail correlation with KV misses

Noise controls and experiment hygiene:
- Pin CPU frequency governor to performance for CI nodes or record governor state.
- Set identical CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and driver stack for baseline vs candidate runs.
- Use fixed random seeds where model sampling is non-deterministic; for stochastic steps, record seed.
- Warmup: always run a 60s warmup with representative trace before collecting metrics.
- Repeat each scenario at least 3 times and report median; if variance > 10% rerun additional samples.

Regression detection (statistical and heuristic):
- Rule-based alert: p99 latency increases by >15% AND kernel-switch rate increased >5x => likely kernel performance regression.
- KV regression: KV hit ratio drop >3% with correlated p95 latency increase => cache invalidation or eviction policy change.
- Scheduling regression: sustained queue_length > (baseline + 2*stddev) with no corresponding increase in incoming rps => scheduling slowdown.
- For CI: mark run as failed if any rule triggers and effect holds across at least 2/3 replicates.

Artifact capture and retention policy:
- For each run, bundle: driver logs, runtime microtrace, sampled GPU kernel traces (via nvprof/NSIGHT-lite), trace input, trace_manifest entry, and a short markdown summary with detected rule triggers.
- Store artifacts on S3 under s3://redwood-perf/elasticity-probes/YYYY-MM-DD/<run-id> and include signed URL in CI output. Keep artifacts for 90 days by default.

Quick-run recipes (dev machine):
- Local quick: ./harness/runner --trace trace_repo/chat_short.json --mode quick --warmup 30 --out ./artifacts/quick1
- CI full scenario: ./harness/runner --trace-matrix traces/matrix.yaml --repeat 3 --collect-kernels --bundle ./artifacts/ci-<sha>

Interpreting outputs (short guidance):
- If p50 stable but p99 regressed, look at taily artifacts: kernel-switch heatmaps and queue snapshots at tail time.
- If throughput drops but single-request latency stable, inspect batching distribution (too many small batches). Scheduler policies may be overly conservative.
- If KV-hit ratio drops after a code change touching KV eviction or sharding, run microbench focused on eviction patterns (controlled insert+read tests).

Known confounders and checklist:
- Driver-level clock skew: ensure monotonic clocks used for timestamps.
- CUDA driver upgrades: always run compatibility smoke after driver changes.
- Host-level noisy neighbors: run GPU isolation checks and record host metrics.
- Model compilation caching: a first-request compile can create a large 1st-request spike—exclude compile time from steady-state metrics.

Runbook / next steps (short-term):
- Add 6 canonical traces to trace_repo with PR: runtime#742 (Arjun assigned).
- Implement kernel-sample exporter (Sofia) to record kernel_name and latency per invocation. Target delivery: 2025-01-20.
- Wire up CI gating in perf pipeline: run the light elasticity probe for every runtime release candidate.
- Ownership: maya@redwood-inference.com for playbook maintenance.

Decision log (why this exists):
- We observed latent regressions that slipped past e2e tests because the signal was in kernel-switch paths and KV interactions; short, focused probes allow quicker turnaround and clearer root cause mapping.

Appendix: quick checklist for running and triage:
- confirm trace chosen from trace_manifest and tag matches PR change
- run warmup, then 3 replicates, then collect artifacts
- run auto-analysis script ./harness/analyze --bundle <bundle> and inspect top-3 correlated signals
- escalate to runtime-oncall with bundle link, short summary, and suspected subsystem

Unresolved questions:
- Should we include multi-tenant interference traces (noisy co-tenants) in the default CI matrix? Pros/cons to discuss.
- Threshold choices for rule-based detection need empirical tuning; propose a 6-week calibration window at rollout.

Notes to self: keep playbook lightweight. If a scenario routinely takes >45m, break it into smaller sub-scenarios for CI.
